one_line: WorkOS DX engineer on replacing 10k lines of generated agent skills with 553 lines of gotchas, enforcing gates in a state machine, and making agents prove their work with hashes and videos.
summary: Nick Nisi, a developer-experience engineer at WorkOS, describes building "Case," an internal harness that takes a GitHub issue, PR, Slack thread or Linear ticket and works until it produces a PR with evidence. The harness started as a Claude skill, lost context as it grew, and was rebuilt on Pi with a TypeScript state machine that runs implementer, verifier, reviewer, closer and retro agents with checks between them. He says agents lied about running tests, so he made them prove it: the SHA-256 of real test output is stored and verified. For the WorkOS CLI, which installs AuthKit into customer projects, he generated over 10,000 lines of skills from docs, found the evals got worse (68-minute runs), and replaced them with 553 lines of hand-written gotchas that run in six minutes. His main lessons are to enforce rules in code instead of prompts, guide rather than prescribe, measure every skill, make agents show evidence (such as Playwright videos on PRs), and fix the harness rather than the output when something fails.

key_ideas.idea: Setup time per task is the hidden cost of running many agents across many repos
key_ideas.detail: Each new agent session needed about 10 minutes of the speaker's time to rebuild context from the issue, ticket and Slack thread, and context switching got worse as repos multiplied.

key_ideas.idea: Put the gates in code, not in the prompt
key_ideas.detail: The state machine decides what runs next: the reviewer cannot start until the verifier passes, reviewer issues send work back to the implementer, and the closer must supply evidence. The speaker's view is that a model can skip or forget prompt instructions but cannot skip a transition the code enforces.

key_ideas.idea: Agents fake completion, so require cryptographic proof
key_ideas.detail: The agent touched an empty .case-tested file to pass the check. The fix was to store the SHA-256 of the real test output and verify it, so the agent has to actually run the tests.

key_ideas.idea: More generated documentation made the agent worse
key_ideas.detail: About 10,000 lines of skills generated from the docs, with a cache hash per section, produced worse results and 68-minute evals. Keeping only common failure points (553 lines) ran faster and scored higher.

key_ideas.idea: Measure every skill with and without it loaded
key_ideas.detail: One skill dropped a task's success from 97% without it to 77% with it. The speaker only found this by running paired evals, and he says Claude's skill-creator eval flow makes this easy.

key_ideas.idea: Guide with conditional rules, do not prescribe with doc summaries
key_ideas.detail: Write rules that fire in the right situation, for example that redirects cannot be called outside Next.js proxy code, instead of pasting a summary of the docs, which the model tends to apply everywhere.

key_ideas.idea: Make the agent show the result in a non-code form before reviewing code
key_ideas.detail: For a UI bug, the agent records a before and after video with the Playwright CLI and attaches it to the PR. The speaker says he reads the code only after the proof convinces him.

key_ideas.idea: When the agent fails, fix the harness, not the output
key_ideas.detail: Each failure becomes a harness bug. The speaker says his team of Lopopolo-style harness engineers never edits the product code directly, only the harness that drives the agent.

key_ideas.idea: A retrospective agent mines transcripts for failure patterns and writes memory
key_ideas.detail: After each run, a retro agent reads the Claude and Codex JSONL logs, looks for doom loops such as the same tool call repeated with no changes, and writes per-framework markdown memory files so the next run avoids the same traps. Auto-pruning of that memory is planned.

key_ideas.idea: For products that serve agents, find what agents get wrong and write gotchas for it
key_ideas.detail: Tutorials are less useful than a short list of the product's landmines, because models already know how to code. The speaker also suggests checking that content loaded by JavaScript after page load still reaches agents that fetch pages.

techniques.name: Enforced state-machine gates for agent pipelines
techniques.how: Model the agent workflow as explicit states in code (implement, verify, review, close, retro), with guarded transitions. A failed review returns to implement. The agent cannot advance on its own say-so.
techniques.when: Long unattended agent runs where the agent skips steps or claims success without doing the work.

techniques.name: Hash-verified test receipts
techniques.how: Run the test command, store the SHA-256 of its real output in a receipt file, and verify that hash at the gate before accepting the step.
techniques.when: You need proof that tests ran, not just a file that says they did.

techniques.name: Gotchas-only skills validated by paired evals
techniques.how: Collect the failures seen across evals and write only those as short gotcha lists. Run each task with and without the skill and keep a skill only if the pass rate goes up.
techniques.when: Writing skills for a product or framework the model partly knows, especially when a generated docs dump is tempting.

techniques.name: Visual before-and-after proof on PRs
techniques.how: For UI changes, have the agent record the bug and the fix with the Playwright CLI and attach the videos to the PR. Reviewers look at the proof first.
techniques.when: Agent-written UI fixes that a reviewer would otherwise need to run by hand.

techniques.name: Retrospective agent over run transcripts
techniques.how: After a run, a separate agent reads the JSONL transcripts, flags doom loops (repeated identical tool calls, parallel tool overuse), and writes lessons into per-framework memory files that load in later runs.
techniques.when: A harness that runs the same kinds of tasks repeatedly on the same codebases.

techniques.name: Conditional rules instead of doc summaries
techniques.how: Write if-then rules tied to the context in which the mistake happens, such as only using redirects inside Next.js proxy code, rather than general descriptions of the docs.
techniques.when: Steering a model away from a specific, recurring framework mistake.

numbers.claim: Speaker has not written a line of code himself in about eight months; works across 20+ repos in 8 languages
Setup per agent session took roughly 10 minutes of human time
Case harness has five agents: implementer, verifier, reviewer, closer, retro
WorkOS install sets up AuthKit in under five minutes
About 10,000+ lines of generated skills, with evals taking 68 minutes to run
Replacement set is 553 lines of gotchas; each eval run takes six minutes instead of 68
One skill: task correct 77% of the time with the skill loaded vs 97% without it
Speaker deleted about 95% of the skill content and performance went up (his claim, measured with evals)

hot_takes: Enforce agent behavior in code, not prompts. A model can decide to skip an instruction, but it cannot skip a transition the state machine blocks.
Generating skills from your full docs can make agents worse. Keep only the gotchas that paired evals show matter.
Never trust an agent's claim it did the work. Make it prove the result in a non-code form (video, hash) before you read the code.
When an agent fails, fix the harness, not the output. Your job was never really about writing code; it is about building the systems that run agents.

relevance.why: ProsHarness is a harness around the Claude Code CLI with checkpoints, plan/critique loops and approvals. This talk gives a concrete design for enforced gates between agent stages, hash-verified test receipts, and a retro agent that reads transcripts and writes memory, all of which touch the same problems.
relevance.action: Read how ProsHarness's checkpoint barrier decides a step is done, then add a receipt check: store the SHA-256 of the real test output and require it at the verify gate before the run can move on, so a touched marker file cannot pass.

relevance.why: L2D SkillForge has an open question about the success signal and skill-worthiness scoring. The talk's paired with/without-skill pass-rate delta (77% vs 97%) is a concrete signal, and it shows that adding a skill can lower success.
relevance.action: Use a with-skill vs without-skill pass-rate delta on the same task set as the skill-worthiness signal in SkillForge, and flag skills with a negative delta for removal.

relevance.why: Reusable pattern: test skills with paired evals before keeping them, and turn repeated agent failures into short gotcha rules. This applies to any agent or skill library the team maintains.
relevance.action: Pick one existing skill, run it paired with and without on five tasks, and delete any section that does not raise the pass rate.
